newsitem.title: UK: NATO in disarray over how to handle Russia.
newsitem.headline: NATO in disarray over how to handle Russia.

text.p: NATO is in disarray over how to handle its difficult relationship with Moscow, with the United States and some other allies distinctly cool about a French-led proposal to hold a summit of major powers with Russia.
The row comes at a sensitive time, as the 16-nation Western alliance tries to overcome Russian objections to NATO's planned expansion into Central and Eastern Europe.
While the shape of a potential deal for a special relationship with Russia is emerging, the problem now is that the allies seem to disagree over the tactics of negotiation.

French President Jacques Chirac, with German support, has floated the idea of a Paris summit in April that would try to work out some of the details of a new relationship between NATO and Russia as the key to European security.
The meeting would include the leaders of Russia, the United States, France, Britain and Germany.

Russia welcomed the idea as a sign that the West was taking its security concerns seriously, since NATO plans to invite the first new states from the former Soviet bloc to apply for membership a few months later, at a summit in Madrid in July.
But Washington, which prides itself on being the main Western partner for Russia, has given the proposal a frosty reception and suggested the Paris meeting will not go ahead.

Some smaller NATO allies are unhappy at the idea of the big powers striking a deal with Russia -- they are still resentful of how the same countries formed a "contact group" which took key decisions on the Yugoslav conflict.

"I can tell you that this whole thing has put a lot of noses out of joint," said one Western envoy, who asked not to be identified. "The Russians must be rubbing their hands with glee at this sort of confusion. It helps them in negotiating."
There are, as ever, questions of power and prestige behind the dispute -- particularly differences between France and the United States over the European role in security issues.
In Washington, U.S. officials said there was concern among smaller countries that they would be left out of vital decisions on the relationship between NATO and Russia.
Diplomats said there was some truth to that view, although one noted tartly that consideration for the views of smaller countries had "not always influenced the Americans so much".
"I don't like this idea much," Belgian Foreign Minister Eric Derycke said bluntly on Wednesday.
"These decisions cannot be taken by small groups of states," said Dutch Foreign Ministry spokesman Gert Kampman.
France and some other European countries are equally worried that the whole issue will be sorted out bilaterally between Washington and Moscow, leaving them out of the loop.
Already locked in disagreement with Washington over the shape of NATO's military command, Paris is suspicious of U.S. intentions and eager to create a stronger European role.

Diplomats say the idea of a Paris summit may now be quietly laid to rest, unless Washington changes its mind. France underlined on Thursday that no decision had been taken, apparently preparing the way for a climbdown.
Meanwhile, Western nations are pursuing negotiations with Moscow as fast as they can, in the hope that they can achieve a deal before the NATO summit in July.

Chirac, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana have been to Moscow in recent weeks. A U.S.-Russian summit is scheduled for next month and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin is in Washington this week.

Russia wants a binding treaty with NATO that would give it an effective veto over important security issues. While the alliance has signalled that this will not be possible, it is putting together a package of measures to reassure Moscow.

This is likely to include assurances about NATO military deployments, a formal relationship providing for regular consultations, arms control measures, financial aid and a boost to Russia's role in fora such as the Group of Seven (G7).
